text: The confidence intervals in the last lesson relied on a formula and on assumptions about shape. Fine for a mean, but what about a median, or a ratio, or the difference between two medians? Formulas for those are messy or nonexistent. The bootstrap treats your sample as a stand-in for the population, resamples from it with replacement over and over, recomputes your statistic each time, and uses the spread of those results to measure uncertainty.

You have one sample of n observations. You can't collect more, but you can imitate that by drawing n observations from your own sample, with replacement — some values repeat, others are left out entirely. That's one bootstrap resample. Compute your statistic on it, repeat thousands of times, and the distribution of that statistic across resamples approximates its true sampling distribution.

Take 40 order values from a skewed distribution — mean 35.32, median only 25.4, a sign of skew. One resample's mean comes out to 32.3. Doing this 10,000 times, the bootstrap standard error of 4.42 closely matches the formula's 4.50. The percentile interval simply takes the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of all those bootstrap means: 27.5 to 44.76.

The t interval on the same data was 26.22 to 44.42. Notice the bootstrap interval sits slightly to the right, reflecting the right skew in the real data, while the t interval is forced to be perfectly symmetric. This is where the bootstrap earns its keep — there's no simple standard-error formula for a median, yet we can bootstrap it anyway.

Drawing all the row indices at once — far faster than a Python loop — the median of 25.4 gets a 95 percent bootstrap interval of roughly 20 to 42.6, with a bootstrap standard deviation of 6.13. That's wide, honestly reflecting how little 40 observations say about the middle of a skewed distribution.

Recent scipy versions include scipy.stats.bootstrap — pass your data and a statistic function, and it does the resampling for you. Its default method, BCa, bias-corrected and accelerated, adjusts for bias and skew, which is why its interval for the mean, 28.76 to 47.59, shifts further right than the plain percentile version.

Bootstrapping really shines for comparing groups. Resample each group separately and record the difference in means — the observed difference is 1.93, but the bootstrap interval runs from about negative 12 to positive 16, comfortably including zero. The data simply cannot distinguish the two groups — a preview of hypothesis testing.

The bootstrap isn't magic. It can't fix a biased or unrepresentative sample — it only resamples what you already have. With very small samples it underestimates uncertainty, and it fails for extreme statistics like the maximum, since the sample max shows up in about 63.5 percent of resamples by construction, not real new information. If observations are dependent — time series, clusters — you must resample whole blocks, not individual rows.

To recap: resample with replacement, recompute, and read the interval off the percentiles. The bootstrap gives standard errors and intervals for medians, ratios, and differences with little math, at the cost of computation and the assumption that your sample truly represents the population. Next, Chapter 5 begins: the logic of hypothesis testing.
